title: Home of a Gamma-ray Pulsar
caption: The surroundings of the gamma-ray pulsar PSR J2030+4415, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: J. Miller (International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Rodriguez (International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab) & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab). Acknowledgments: M. de Vries & R. Romani (Stanford University)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This cloudy field in the direction of Cygnus hides the gamma-ray pulsar PSR J2030+4415, an object the human eye cannot detect. The image was taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on the Gemini North telescope in Hawai‘i. Evidence of a shock front can be seen in the upper left quarter of the frame.

A pulsar is a highly magnetized, rapidly spinning neutron star, the collapsed core left behind when a star 10–25 times more massive than the Sun dies in a supernova. Neutron stars pack roughly 1.5 times the Sun's mass into a sphere about 12 miles across, so dense that a teaspoon of their material would weigh as much as Mount Everest.

As a pulsar spins, it sends beams of radiation out from its poles, gamma rays in this case. When a beam sweeps across Earth, astronomers see it flash at regular intervals, like a lighthouse. The surrounding haze is a pulsar wind nebula, made of material shed by the supernova and blown around by winds from the pulsar.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with GMOS on Gemini North through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The pulsar's gamma rays are completely invisible to the eye. The image shows only the visible glow of the surrounding nebula.
